title: Notes of Ministry - 78 - May 1979

source.file: Various/Notes of Ministry - 78 - May 1979 (2490)/Notes of Ministry - 78 - May 19 - Various.epub

paragraphs.text: I have thought recently, beloved brethren, that we can well do with some stimulation as to the coming of the Lord. I have observed that it is not as much spoken of as it should be. It should be the hope of our hearts that we are waiting for Him. It is said of some of our early brethren that they “turned to God from idols to serve a living and true God, and to await his Son from the heavens”, 1 Thessalonians 1: 9, 10. If we were to speak in the language of the parable of the bridegroom we might well say, ‘He is on His way’. That is something to think about, and to govern our affections. His coming is near— how near, we could say. It is not just the fact of His coming, but who is coming. I wonder whether love for Christ has so gripped our hearts that we want Him? We miss Him and we want Him at the Supper. He is absent from this scene. He has gone out by way of death, and we want Him; we miss Him. What it will be when He comes! The creation groans—the bondage will be lifted; the sorrows and the sufferings will be over; the present condition of christendom, as our brother has said, finished with. How we long for that! But I wonder how much we think of what the Lord is looking for; whether we can furnish what is attractive to the Lord, that which caused Him to say in the word to Philadelphia, “I come quickly”, Revelation 3: 11. Would we not like to furnish the Lord with what will meet the longings of His heart? And what will meet them save to see Himself over again?

Our minds revert to the prime type of the assembly in Genesis 2 and the Lord saying, in type, “This time ...”. Every living creature had come under Adam’s eye, but when he saw Eve he said, “This time it is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh”, he saw himself, as it has been said, over again. I am sure that is what the Lord is after. I think it was there in Philadelphia, and therefore He says, “I make them ... know that I have loved thee”. What is it the Lord loves? He loves what is of Himself, and so He looks down at the Supper and sees a few gathered; they miss Him. They are thankful indeed for the forgiveness of their sins; thankful for salvation experienced in the testimony, for deliverance from the world and from the flesh and all that stands related to that order of things, but, more than that, He finds hearts that miss Him and want Him. You see the breathing of it in Mr. Darby’s hymns; his heart longed for Christ, and I think our hearts may well be stimulated, dear brethren, to long a little more for Him, not just for the relief so far as we are concerned, but for the great Lover of our souls, to be with Him and like Him, but to furnish Him with what He has long sought in the affection of the assembly.

So I read the passage in 2 Corinthians 4: 11 because that is exactly what it is—“That the life also of Jesus may be manifested in our mortal flesh”. It is a wonderful thing that the life of Jesus can come out in expression in our bodies here, in the condition in which we are of mortal flesh. So He sees the brethren come up to the prayer meeting, and what does He see?

Our brother has been speaking of persevering in prayer. What did He see when they came up at Philippi? What did He see in that prison when Paul and Silas, under the sufferings of the lash, their backs smitten, lifted up their voice and in praying were praising? He saw Himself over again—the praying Man. What did He see in Stephen as he died and lifted up his voice to the Lord and said, “Lord, lay not this sin to their charge”? What that must have meant to the heart of Christ, to see His own features coming to light, the work of the Spirit. We have it too in Philippians 1: 19, where Paul says, “I know that this shall turn out to me to salvation, through your supplication and the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ”—what a reflection of Christ—not only a reflection, it is Christ over again really; that is what came to light in the assembly at Philippi; through suffering, through pressure, but through the formation of the Spirit, the very spirit of Christ came into expression.

Well, that is Philadelphia, whether it be in prayer, or in testimony, and if the life of Jesus is seen in our mortal flesh, then it will be that something of the radiancy that is in His face will shine in us. Maybe we are rejected; maybe others will not have anything to do with us. Does it affect the fact that our faces are going to shine anyway? We are going to maintain the spirit of the new covenant; we are going to show the radiancy of the glory that shines in the face of Jesus now. So the Spirit is in us down here not only that we go through in victory, but I think that what He is after is to see worked out in expression in the beloved saints what is of Christ Himself, the life of Jesus seen in our mortal flesh.

Now that is what is going to attract the Lord. I think that is what He saw in Philadelphia, which, it has been said, He will credit to the whole assembly. We are not thinking just of ourselves, but it can work out in the twos and threes, the life of Jesus. He says, “I know thy works—behold, I have set before thee an opened door”. There is

the service of God on the one hand and then the keeping of His word and not denying His name, meaning that the service of God and the testimony go on together. It means so much to the Lord, the keeping of His word, that He says, “I will cause that they shall ... know that I have loved thee”; it is not only that He loves what they had done, but “I have loved thee”. I think that is as the assembly has come to love Christ, and He has seen Himself over again in the assembly, and He says, “I have loved thee”, and He wants the assembly. I think that is why He says in this section, “I come quickly”. Speaking reverently, He will not hold Himself back. He says, ‘That is what I want, and that is what I am going to rapture’. Can we furnish the Lord, in the setting in which we are, with features that are so attractive to Him that He will come quickly? If He does not immediately rapture us He will come by His word; He will come at the Supper; He will come into our households; but what more could we enjoy than the sense of the Lord’s approval, that as He comes there is something that He has longed for and has found?

We retain, I trust, impressions from the meetings in this city last October, the substance of which I think we shall allow to run out of us only to our loss. My own impression is that the Lord had something to say to His people in those meetings which was intended to be of the very greatest value to them. In fact, although on previous occasions we have had much that has been distinctive as to doctrine, and distinctly helpful to the saints in that regard (for the recapitulation of doctrine is always valuable to the saints, both to keep them in the right way and indeed as food for them, insofar as doctrine sets out and outlines the truth), what the Lord had to say to us is something that relates to what is organic and establishing among the saints, bearing especially on our relations with one another, and in my judgment underlying in a very substantial way the whole of our experience as in fellowship together. I believe that if the Lord says something to us about these things we shall overlook it at our peril.

The thought which our beloved brother brought in at the beginning of ‘communicative associations’ (See ‘Notes and Comments’, J. N. Darby, Vol. 7, p.1), is important in itself and bears on the degree in which we actually communicate with one another in regard to the truth, in regard to impressions of Christ; you might even say the degree to which we are able to feed one another. I know that the word may have another meaning in its strict translation but we should not forget the literal interpretation of the words in English, “of doing good and communicating ... be not forgetful”, Hebrews 13: 16. Brethren will recall too that our brother introduced another word and with it another thought; that was the word ‘social’. (It seems necessary when one uses the word ‘social’ always to say ‘in its right sense’, although the saints should always interpret words in their right sense). I believe there is something to be gained by us all in that regard too.

I have therefore referred especially to Luke 24 with reference to “part of a ... honeycomb”, because as is well known the hive in nature is perhaps the best representation of a social system. Its characteristics are clear—one of its main characteristics is that each is working for the gain of the whole and in relation to a whole, and each is working and serving in order to maintain what is whole in that system.

Another interesting detail is that the honeycomb, which is the next entity, as it were, from the hive, is perfect in itself, made up of regular hexagons, as if they had been measured by the most refined instruments, and each exact. It bears on the perfection of the way in which things are related together in the divine system, if we may transfer the thought; and the honey flows from that. Of course, the hive and the honeycomb have elements which we would not expect to find in the christian circle; that is, it has an element of bees that do not work at all. We would never expect to find that. It also has a queen; you would never expect to find them.

But leaving that aside, the structure itself represents to us, I believe, something in which we can even discern what may represent to us the working of the body, a thing about which we often speak but about which we perhaps know less in practice than we speak of. Let us test ourselves even as to “if one member suffer, all the members suffer” (1 Corinthians 12: 26); I challenge myself as to how much I suffer with anyone who suffers. For instance, a brother who was with us at the week-end is out of work—how much do I suffer with him? Think of those who are sick and ill and old—how much do I suffer with them? Think too of those who rejoice—how much do I rejoice with them? It says, “Rejoice, young man, in thy youth”, Ecclesiastes 11: 9. How much do I rejoice with the youths and with the young sisters? How much am I working out in character the actuality of what is represented in the body?

We do not need to say that the body represents that in which no breakdown is possible—it is that. That is something that remains absolute. There is no possibility of breakdown in the body of Christ. The Holy Spirit is here, the one Spirit, and because He is here there is no possibility of breakdown. We might say, Thank God for that! Because it gives us inherently an inward link with that which can never break down. If we look at what relates to responsibility we might excuse anyone who said there was only discouragement, but if we look at what belongs to the Spirit and what is in the Spirit, we are inherently in touch with what cannot break down. That is the key to the establishment and enjoyment of this social structure which the body represents. On the other hand, there is the side of responsibility, and the natural order of things to which I am referring has many lessons for us in relation to responsibility, because the system of things which the hive and the bees represent raises with us the question how far each of us is committed, wholly committed, devoted, and actually applying ourselves, to the working of this great system of things which is intended to be so edifying and comforting and sustaining.

In responsibility we have something to do to see that we are maintaining it, and I think that that would be one reason why the Lord gives us ministry in that regard, to test us as to the working of our responsibility in such a system of things. As I have said already, we may work it out in consideration for one another, consideration for the old, and consideration for those who may be feeble. We pray as we gather, as we have tonight, for those who are not able to be here and they are in our thoughts. We gather them up; in a certain sense we seek to enjoy the occasion with them although they are not here. We have them in our thoughts. Then there are the young and those growing up, those making their way, those at work and those out in the world, at least during the day; the same structure embraces them and we are tested as to how far we are able to embrace one another in this secure system.

That is an impression I have as to it, that it is a secure system, and we are tested as to whether the links we have with one another are as perfect as they are in this natural object to which I am referring. The link of each cell with the next is perfect and, beloved, we are all tested as to whether our links with one another have that quality of perfection. If, for instance, I was next to a different cell from what I am habitually, would my links with that cell be as perfect as they are with those to whom I am customarily attached? or do I find it easier to fit in some areas than others? If I do, I am not a good bee in that sense, because the structure of the honeycomb rests on its regularity. I think that if we reflect on the thought of what is social as related to the christian company we shall find that it bears on the ability we have to sustain relations with one another in a supportive, protective, but productive way, so that all get the gain and all are blessed through it.

The Lord would help us in these things, I believe. When He came in in resurrection to this company He said, “Have ye anything here to eat?” It is a very remarkable thing that they had part of a honeycomb. I know that the scripture bears other interpretations and other applications, but this was a locality. We have been taught from Luke 24: 36, where He came and stood in their midst, that it bears on the locality, and in a locality you could not have the whole honeycomb. It requires all the saints for the whole thing; but they had part of it. As we often say in our localities, we are part of that great whole. They had part of a honeycomb. I do not in any way set aside other applications of this scripture which bear on the weakness of the time, but they had part of a honeycomb, and we might ask ourselves, beloved, if the Lord came in corporeally in London, would we be able to say we gave Him part of a broiled fish and of a honeycomb?

That is to say, we had this blessed social system thoroughly working among us in support and sustaining, protection and production, so that we were here able to offer the Lord something which He was ready to eat before us. The Lord never made any comment, He did not criticise anything that they offered Him. It says, “he took it and ate before them”. We often wonder at the Lord’s grace, but I believe, beloved, that if He finds a system of things like this working, even in a locality, the Lord would take it and eat it before us to show us that He enjoys being in a circle where these things are enjoyed.

I have referred to Jonathan. I scarcely need to remind the brethren of other scriptures relating to honey, some of them careful scriptures, advising us to be careful and warning us, helping us. “Hast thou found honey? Eat so much as is sufficient for thee”, Proverbs 25: 16. That is to say it is something whose place has to be learned. Lower down in the same chapter it says, “It is not good to eat much honey “(verse 27). It goes on to say very interestingly that “to search into weighty matters is itself a weight”. It is a very interesting remark. It is not good to eat too much, and we know that it was not a thing that was to be offered to God. I can understand that; we often apply it in relation to what is naturally sweet, but we do not exactly offer to God our relationships with one another; we offer to God, out of those relationships, things which are affecting for Him, powerful towards Him and yielding something for Him. We keep these scriptures that warn us as to the right place of these things in our minds, but the land into which the children of Israel were going flowed with milk and honey. I believe, as a matter of fact, that if you look up the references to honey you will find that the majority of them are to milk and honey in the land. It shows that this is something that God expected the people to enjoy; indeed, He provided it for them. They would find that when they went there, a land flowing with milk and honey.

As I have said, I believe the hive represents this great social structure in which we have part, and are intended to have part; the honeycomb is in a sense the demonstration of it and the honey is the product of it. Jonathan says, “See, I pray you, that mines eyes are bright, because I tasted a little of this honey”. Beloved brethren, how attractive it becomes! It is the product of these things working blessedly among the brethren, and working positively, working encouragingly and working productively—Oh he only took a little and his eyes were bright!

How much honey can you get on the end of a stick anyway? Not very much, but it says “he put forth the end of his staff which was in his hand, and dipped it in the honeycomb, and put his hand to his mouth, and his eyes became bright” (1 Samuel 14: 27). Beloved, why should not our eyes become bright? Why should any of us on any occasion be dull? Why should we?

If we are dull, we shall have to go back to the scripture in Genesis on which our beloved brother preached. That is, If thou doest well, will not thy countenance look up with confidence? and if thou doest not well, a sin-offering lies at the door.

But why should our eyes not be bright? I believe that if the blessedness of this system of social relationships—in the Lord, need I say, and reflecting those relationships that are regulated and governed by the power of the Spirit—were among us we would find that our eyes became bright, and that the whole system of things amongst us, the meetings, all that proceeds (we come together very often) on each occasion, reflected the fact that our eyes were bright. Beloved, you could ask yourself and I could ask myself—we all no doubt have a mirror somewhere—Are my eyes bright? And if they are not, why not? If your eyes are not bright, why not? It may be that you need to taste honey—in its right setting. I will allow for all the scriptures that regulate and govern this; we cannot leave any scripture out and none is of a private interpretation, but Jonathan says, “See, I pray you, that mine eyes are bright, because I tasted a little of this honey”. It was the product of that system of things which subsists in nature, subsists instinctively in nature; nobody tells the bees what to do, it subsists instinctively, and it should subsist amongst us instinctively in the power of the Spirit.

Jonathan found its product. The land flowed with it and he dipped the end of his staff in it and he ate it, and his eyes became bright. And while he goes on to say, “How much more, if the people had eaten freely today of the spoil of their enemies”, I think that what he is trying to communicate to Saul is, If you had only let them all eat this honey what a day this would have been, we would certainly have ravaged the Philistines.

But think of Israel with everyone’s eyes bright! It will not come about, beloved, until the millennium. You will find that in Isaiah, “Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf be

unstopped” (Isaiah 35: 5). That is the day when all Israel’s eyes will be bright, but, beloved, our eyes may be bright because we are enjoying the blessed productiveness of this system of things in which the Lord has placed us and in which the Spirit is the binding power so that these things may be enjoyed.

I just say this out of desire to communicate to the brethren impressions that I at least have retained from the meetings we had last month and that in the Lord’s grace it might be productive among us.

What is precious in Scripture and in the rich, spiritual ministry that the Lord has given, and continues to give, in the present recovery lies beneath the surface, and to get this wealth requires “manual labour”, Proverbs 13: 11. This means that we follow up what we read in the Scriptures, or what we listen to or read in the ministry, with deep and diligent exercise in secret with God, so as to be formed thereby and to increase in spiritual wealth. If the word of God does not affect us morally, then what we gather is mere mental knowledge which puffs up, and is like what is spoken of in the first part of the verse—wealth gotten by vanity, which diminishes. The ever-present tendency to ease, self-indulgence, and lethargy, needs to be overcome in the power of the Holy Spirit, who also helps us to search out spiritual riches, for “the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God”, 1 Corinthians 2: 10. The description of mining in Job 28 shows us that the great spiritual riches suggested in the valuable metals and precious stones mentioned are only secured by manual labour and going deep, even to the utmost limit.
Spiritual wealth thus acquired is true and durable and serves to enrich the assembly now; it will remain to shine in its lustre eternally for the glory of God.
Lossiemouth

I want to say something about friends. I suppose we have all got a friend. No matter how young you are, I expect you have a friend; somebody you can confide in, somebody you can trust. It is good to have friends you can trust. I want to speak about a Friend who, the scripture says, “sticketh closer than a brother” (Proverbs 18: 24). One you can trust at all times. You could not have a better friend than Jesus. Do you know Jesus as your Friend? He is a Friend who will stand by you. When it is not easy, when things are difficult, He will stand by you.
When He came here persons did not recognise Him for what He was. He came here to be a Friend of persons. It says in the first verse we read “a friend of tax-gatherers and sinners”.

Jesus came to be the Friend of persons in need. You hardly require a friend if you have not a need. If you have no need you are self-sufficient, you become your own centre and your own object. But if you have a need you require a friend you can trust. Jesus came to be the Friend you can trust. Luke’s gospel presents Him like that. Jesus came in to be the Friend of every man, woman, boy and girl. He did not come in in pomp and splendour; no, He came in in lowly guise. To be a Friend He came near. That is how Jesus has approached us. He came to be near you. Luke’s gospel particularly brings out Jesus coming alongside the sinner, alongside the needy. If anybody had a need, if anybody had a want, if anybody was dissatisfied, Jesus came alongside. Oh what a Friend! Do you know a Friend like that—“A friend of tax-gatherers and sinners”? Are you a sinner? If you are, Jesus came to be your Friend. He came to take up your case. “Wisdom”, it says, “has been justified of all her children”. This is wisdom’s way.
Who would have devised things like this? made such an arrangement that there could be a Friend just there when you needed Him?

That is what the man found on the Jericho road. It says that a certain man descended from Jerusalem to Jericho. Now the downward road is a very easy road to tread. It is always more difficult to go uphill, to go against the stream. It is easy when things are downhill, and generally when things are easy we think they are good. I would judge that this man when he left Jerusalem thought that everything was going to be all right; but on the road down he fell into the hands of robbers. They stripped him, wounded him, and left him half dead lying by the wayside—and he had no friend. He could not help himself; he was half dead. What this man needed was a friend, somebody who would come near. Our position in our sins is that we are without hope and without God in the world. That is just where we are. No hope! What could this man do? What could any one of us do to meet one of our sins—not to speak of the many we have? A hopeless case!

Jesus came alongside this man. That is what He does today in the gospel; Jesus comes alongside the sinner, “a friend of tax-gatherers and sinners”. It says, “a certain Samaritan”, that is Jesus! There is “a certain priest” and a Levite, but there is “a certain Samaritan”. Oh what a Friend is Jesus! It says he came up to him. I never tire of speaking of Jesus coming up to persons. We may talk down to people or look down on people. The Friend I want to speak about comes up to you. He has been lower, a Friend who has gone right to the bottom. The whole question of our sins, our guilt, our debt—Jesus has gone right to the bottom to meet it, and He comes up to the person in need.

Oh what a Saviour is Jesus! Do you know a friend like this—a Friend who will take you on when nobody else wants you? That is what this man found. The priest passed by, the Levite passed by. Men try all their ideas of reform to meet the problems. They have introduced a great deal of social reform to try to better man in his conditions, and what happens? The same old thing exists, and what do they do? They just have to leave it, pass by, try to cover it up.

But Jesus comes right to the needy. Have you known the touch of Jesus as He comes up to you? It says he bound up the man’s wounds. You know, sin inflicts wounds; it leaves marks. Jesus would bind them up, and not only that, but He pours in oil and wine. That is Jesus, the Friend with resource. What a Friend to have—One who has abundance of supply. He has all that you need and He carries it all with Him. All the resource and supply of heaven is available to the sinner who believes in Jesus. Is He not worth trusting? Have you a need that would make you want to trust Him? I think that is the difficulty often. We resist, we kick against things because we do not feel the need. This man was half dead. What could he do? He could do nothing for himself so he was entirely dependent on the friend who came near. ‘Who was neighbour?’ That is the word. Who was friend to the man on the wayside? The one that showed mercy.

Paul says, “but ... mercy was shewn me”, 1 Timothy 1: 16. Was he not the man on the wayside? The Lord arrested him from glory; He stopped him in his path; but He bound up his wounds, pouring in oil and wine, and He put him on his own beast, “Rise up and enter into the city, and it shall be told thee what thou must do”, Acts 9: 6. There he found the inn, did he not? The Lord directed Ananias to seek out Saul—“he is praying, and has seen in a vision a man by name Ananias coming in and putting his hand on him”, Acts 9: 12. Ananias goes in and that is just what he does. That is the inn; it is a place of safety and salvation. There is an Ananias there who will just put his hand on you.

He took him to the inn and took care of him. Saul of Tarsus was taken care of at Damascus. If we had had anything to do with Saul’s conversion I do not know whether we would have taken him to Damascus! God puts you in the most favoured circumstances. He took him right to that very place, and I suggest there are no more favoured circumstances than those you are in just where you are now. That is where Saul found himself, right in Damascus, and he found the most tender hearts there. When persecution arose they lowered him in a basket. The inn is the most wonderful place.
It is the place where Jesus takes His friends. Do you know that place? Do you enjoy that area, an area of peace, of rest and relaxation? What is the occupation there? Jesus, the Son of God!
That is what Paul preached, “Jesus that he is the Son of God”, the centre of another world.
The whole world system was brought down in the death of Christ and Saul of Tarsus learned in Damascus that wonderful area of salvation.

When we come to Luke 11 it says, “Who among you shall have a friend, and shall go to him at midnight ...?”. Jesus is available all the time. When I call, He will answer. Jesus is available at any time. If you have a need, as we were saying, have you a friend who can supply just what is needed? I do not think we get things in bulk, if I can use that expression.

We get grace as we need it, it is “grace upon grace”. If we got too much we would become independent. But what I want to show you is that there is a Friend who is available to you as the need arises. Just when you are in need, and you do not see the way out, and do not see where to go, you can turn to Him and He will give you what you need. I know this scripture has other applications, but I just want to make this point that there is a Friend available.

“Who among you shall have a friend, and shall go to him at midnight and say to him, Friend, let me have three loaves ...?”. I would like to ask you, Have you ever asked Jesus for anything? Have you ever felt you had to go to Him because you had a need which no other could satisfy? So often we try something else, but finally we have to come to Jesus. He has the wherewithal, He has the resource, He has the supply. He is dispensing from glory today all that is needed to meet your case.

In this well-known section in Luke 15 what is emphasized is that when the lost sheep is found, and when the lost piece of silver is found, the friends and the neighbours are called together. Have you ever been at one of those meetings where all the friends and the neighbours are together?

“Rejoice with me”; somebody who was lost has been found! Wonderful meetings, these! The Lord calls such meetings together. This sheep had got away but He went after it. It says that, having lost one of them, he leaves the ninety and nine in the wilderness and goes after that which is lost, “until he find it”. Luke makes no provision for not finding it. Then he calls in all the friends and the neighbours, saying, “Rejoice with me”. The work is all His, but He calls the friends together. Oh what a time of rejoicing it is when someone is found! Has He found you? Then He will call the friends together and He will say, “Rejoice with me, for I have found my lost sheep”. The woman says, “Rejoice with me, for I have found the drachma which I had lost”. It was out of circulation, but now the friends and the neighbours are all called in.

There is an area where repentance is enjoyed, an atmosphere in which repentance deepens, and all the friends and all the neighbours delight to come in and rejoice because what was lost has been found. The scripture adds, “There shall be joy in heaven for one repenting sinner, more than for ninety and nine righteous who have no need of repentance”; and “There is joy before the angels of God for one repenting sinner”. A repenting sinner is one who has found a Friend. Have you found a Friend? As you are repenting you will find a Friend.

The younger son thought everything was going his way. He got what he wanted and off he went. Then he discovered that he was in want. Have you ever felt you had everything you wanted, and then discovered that it was not really what you wanted at

all? That is what this younger son found. He thought he had got all that he had set his heart upon, and then he found it was empty. But he came to himself. Have you ever sat down just to reason things out? God says, ‘I will reason with you’ (see Isaiah 1: 18). That is grace. God comes so close to us. He will reason with us; He will show us the truth. I think that is how this man came to himself. He says, ‘In my father’s house there is abundance, and here am I; I have nothing’. Immediately he made a move, the father ran. The activities of divine Persons are wonderful. Someone referred this morning to the Lord coming in, “Leaping upon the mountains, Skipping upon the hills” (Song of Songs 2: 8), the agility of Christ as He comes in among His own. Think—we speak reverently—of the Father’s agility in relation to a repenting sinner. The father ran. God sees the first move on your part and He is right there!
You come to yourself and God is right there.

“Bring out the best robe and clothe him in it”, this is what God has always had in mind. You say, ‘I thought the younger son had had his share. What would be left?’ Divine love in purpose has things that “eye has not seen, and ear not heard, and which have not come into man’s heart, which God has prepared”, 1 Corinthians 2: 9. They were there all the time.

“Bring out the best robe and clothe him in it”—a person who is repenting can be clothed in the worth of Christ, a ring on his hand and sandals on his feet; God would dignify the sinner who believes in Jesus. He would put you in all the dignity of sonship, with the token of endless love, which I think the ring would represent, the love of God shed abroad in your heart by the Holy Spirit given. “And bring the fatted calf and kill it and let us eat and make merry: for this, my son was dead and has come to life, was lost and has been found”. The friends are
joining in the merriment over one repenting sinner.

Now there is a warning I want to refer to. The chapter concludes with a man who wanted something to enjoy with his friends. I would just like to ask, ‘Who are your friends?’ This man said (Luke 15: 29)—“To me hast thou never given a kid that I might make merry with my, friends”— my friends. He wanted his own company, but I tell you this, if you want to choose your own company be sure you are on the wrong road. God does not let us choose our company, He chooses it for us. That is what this elder son missed. He missed the fact that God provides the best. You may say, ‘Well, if it was only somebody else who was local; if only so-and-so was not in our meeting’. God chose him to be there. God put him there. He is one of the friends. Get round about him and you might find another side to him. Perhaps you are missing something that God has put there; you have not seen it yet. He is one of the friends and neighbours. There is a great system of help, a system of power, a system of blessing. It is there on your behalf. Make sure you do not miss it.

articles.title: “THE CHERUBIM OF GLORY SHADOWING THE MERCY-SEAT”
articles.author: G. A. Brown

paragraphs.text: The banished pair their journey took
Beyond the garden’s bound.
No more their guileless, happy ways
Would in its groves be found.
Through dalliance with the ancient foe
They disobeyed God’s word;
Lo! at the garden’s eastern gate
Flames the cherubic sword!
When Israel, freed from Egypt’s thrall,
Traversed the desert dry,
Moses, the man of God, received
The pattern from on high.
The holy ark, in every part
With purest gold replete,
The cherubim their wings spread o’er
And faced the mercy-seat.
Then came the great atonement day,
Iniquity laid bare;
They looked upon the mercy-seat
The blood was sprinkled there!
In later days great David’s son,
Secure upon his throne,
Raised up a house unto his God
Of hewn and costly stone.
Wide spread their wings and firm their feet
Within the sacred place—
God’s righteousness and truth set forth,
Toward the house they face!
Oh concept grand! Oh thought divine!
Justice and mercy meet;
God’s rights maintained, His love made known,
In Christ the Mercy-seat!
Edinburgh

“THY WAY” In Psalm 77 Asaph makes two remarkable statements—“O God, thy way is in the sanctuary”, and then later, “Thy way is in the sea, and thy paths are in the great waters; and thy footsteps are not known”. The secret of the divine way is to be found in the sanctuary, in the presence of God. His way is unchanging and is ever related to His eternal purpose for His own. In the sanctuary we understand the heavenly order of things in which all is related to Christ and headed up in Him to the glory of God. Each believer has been predestinated to be conformed to the image of His Son, and the table of shewbread speaks of the way in which God views His own as in Christ before Him. We leave the sanctuary with the comfort and assurance that all the ways of God with us in our lives are surely related to the divine purposes we have contemplated within. We cannot trace the exact detail of what God is working out in all that He allows—Paul says, “How ... untraceable his ways!”
(Romans 11: 33)—but faith has the absolute assurance that His way in the sea and His paths in the great waters are all operating in divine love and skill to secure His glorious purpose.

This gives the greatest comfort in bereavement, pain, anxiety, and weakness. It also helps us to see the lesser perplexities, disappointments, and worries of life in a different light. God would draw us near to Him in these experiences, that we might go through them with Him, assured that He is working out rich and precious formation after Christ which is to adorn His sanctuary and subsist for His pleasure and glory eternally.

How often do we see links with the world formed, or links with believers not walking in the truth, either by marriage or friendship, or by association for mutual advantage, sometimes even by joining in worldly pleasures, or by the reading of worldly literature! If these things go on, “the holy seed” does not preserve its own distinctiveness and separation, and the consequences are spiritually disastrous. For these things being carried on are clear evidence of unfaithfulness to the Lord.
paragraphs.source: C. A. Coates (‘Outline of Mark’s Gospel’, p.242)

paragraphs.text: Because of my infirmity I require His grace and mercy where I am. He is able to help me for He was once here; but He is above everything now and He would have me to know Him where there are no winds and waves and to enjoy Him there. May each of us answer to His love more and more as we apprehend by the Spirit what it is to be with Him where He is, and to set our affections there!

I think we should benefit those we come in contact with very much more, because out of my belly should flow living waters. It ought to be an exercise to everybody that he should be in this world beneficially, he ought not to stagnate. There is something for everyone to do—a man may show mercy with cheerfulness.
